UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical Anatomy:
Why this matters: almost every upper-limb clinical scenario comes down to a nerve, a vessel, or a bone in the wrong place at the wrong time. A fracture at a predictable site injures a predictable nerve, producing a predictable deformity and sensory loss. Learn the site → nerve → motor loss → sensory loss → deformity chain and most OSCE and written questions fall out of it.

Two look-alikes you must separate. Hand of benediction = a high median lesion, seen only when the patient tries to make a fist (index & middle stay extended). Ulnar claw = an ulnar lesion, seen at rest (ring & little finger hyperextend at the MCP, flex at the IP joints). Benediction is active; claw is resting.
The Deformities — Recognise Them on Sight
✋ Wrist drop — Radial nerve
  • All wrist/finger extensors paralysed → wrist and fingers hang flexed
  • Cause: midshaft humeral # (nerve in the spiral groove) or prolonged arm-over-chair compression (“Saturday night palsy”)
  • A high lesion also weakens triceps; a low (posterior interosseous) lesion spares wrist extension but causes finger drop
🙏 Hand of benediction — Median nerve
Benediction: Kencf0618, CC BY-SA 4.0 (posture demonstration). Ape hand: Emily Barrett, CC BY 3.0. Both via Wikimedia Commons.
  • On making a fist, the index & middle fingers cannot flex (lost FDS/FDP + lateral lumbricals) — they stay pointing
  • Chronic: thenar wasting + “ape hand” (thumb pulled into the plane of the palm, lost opposition)
  • High lesion = elbow (supracondylar #); low lesion = wrist (carpal tunnel)
🤚 Ulnar claw — Ulnar nerve
  • Ring & little finger: hyperextended at MCP, flexed at IP (lost medial 2 lumbricals/interossei, unopposed long flexors/extensors)
  • Ulnar paradox: a higher (elbow) lesion gives a less obvious claw — because medial FDP is also paralysed, so the fingertips can’t curl. The claw worsens as a distal lesion or as a proximal one recovers.
  • Froment’s sign: to grip paper the patient flexes FPL (median) to compensate for a weak adductor pollicis
🪽 Winged scapula — Long thoracic nerve
  • Serratus anterior paralysed → medial scapular border lifts off the chest wall, worse on pushing against a wall
  • Also loses the ability to raise the arm above 90° (scapular rotation)
  • Classic cause: axillary node clearance / mastectomy
Benediction vs ulnar claw — the classic mix-up. They look alike (ring & little bent, index & middle straighter), but they are opposite nerves shown at opposite moments. The trick is to ask which fingers are the faulty ones.
🙏 Benediction = MEDIAN
  • Only when making a fist (active)
  • The straight fingers (index + middle) are the faulty ones — median can’t flex them
  • = failure to flex
🤚 Ulnar claw = ULNAR
  • Present at rest (no effort)
  • The bent fingers (ring + little) are the faulty ones — clawed
  • = failure to extend
One-liner: Benediction = can’t make a fist (median). Claw = can’t straighten out (ulnar).
Brachial Plexus Injuries
👶 Erb’s palsy — upper trunk (C5–C6)
  • Mechanism: excessive head–shoulder separation — shoulder dystocia at birth, or a fall onto the shoulder in adults
  • Lost: abductors + external rotators + elbow flexors/supinators
  • Posture: arm adducted, internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated = “waiter’s tip”
  • Roots: C5–C6 (“Erb–six”)
✊ Klumpke’s palsy — lower trunk (C8–T1)
  • Mechanism: excessive abduction — grabbing something when falling, or arm pulled overhead at birth
  • Lost: all the small muscles of the hand (intrinsics)
  • Posture: claw hand
  • May injure the nearby sympathetic T1 fibres → Horner’s syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis)
Plexus roadmap — “Randy Travis Drinks Cold Beer”: Roots → Trunks → Divisions → Cords → Branches. Roots C5–T1; three trunks (upper/middle/lower); each splits into anterior & posterior divisions; three cords (lateral, posterior, medial — named by their relation to the axillary artery); then the five terminal branches (musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median, ulnar).

Scaphoid — the fracture you must not miss. Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox after a FOOSH is scaphoid # until proven otherwise. Its blood supply enters distally (dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery) and runs retrograde, so a proximal-pole fracture starves the proximal fragment → AVN & non-union. It is often invisible on the initial X-ray — if clinically suspected, immobilise in a thumb spica and re-image (repeat X-ray or MRI) in 10–14 days. Never discharge as “sprain”.
Nerve Compression Syndromes

Carpal Tunnel Syndrome — median nerve at the wrist

🧱 The tunnel
  • Roof = flexor retinaculum; floor/walls = carpal bones
  • Contents = 9 tendons + median nerve (4× FDS, 4× FDP, 1× FPL)
  • The palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the tunnel → sensation over the thenar skin is spared in CTS (key discriminator)
🩺 Clinical
  • Paraesthesia of the lateral 3½ fingers, worse at night, shaken out
  • Late: thenar wasting, weak thumb abduction/opposition
  • Tests: Tinel’s (tap) & Phalen’s (flex) reproduce symptoms
  • Causes — “MEDIAN TRAP”: pregnancy, hypothyroid, diabetes, RA, acromegaly, obesity, dialysis
  • Mx: wrist splint → steroid injection → carpal tunnel decompression (divide the retinaculum)
Cubital tunnel — ulnar at the elbow
  • Ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle (the “funny bone”)
  • Numb medial 1½ fingers, weak grip/pinch, clawing
  • Worse with sustained elbow flexion (leaning on the elbow)
Guyon’s canal — ulnar at the wrist
  • Ulnar nerve + artery between pisiform & hook of hamate
  • “Cyclist’s palsy” — handlebar pressure; also ganglia
  • Spares the dorsal ulnar skin (its dorsal branch leaves proximally)
Shoulder — Dislocation & the Rotator Cuff
🎯 Dislocation
  • Anterior (~95%) — arm abducted + externally rotated; risks the axillary nerve (check regimental-badge sensation & deltoid before and after reduction)
  • Posterior — seizures, electrocution, shock; “lightbulb sign” on X-ray
  • Bony Bankart / Hill–Sachs lesions predispose to recurrence
💪 Rotator cuff — “SITS”
  • Supraspinatus — initiates abduction (0–15°); most commonly torn / impinged
  • Infraspinatus — external rotation
  • Teres minor — external rotation
  • Subscapularis — internal rotation
  • Painful arc 60–120° suggests supraspinatus impingement
Vascular Access, the Cubital Fossa & Compartment Syndrome
Cubital fossa — “TAN” (lateral→medial)
  • Tendon of biceps · Arterial (brachial) · Nerve (median)
  • Roof holds the median cubital vein — the standard venepuncture site
  • Borders: pronator teres (medial), brachioradialis (lateral), intercondylar line (superior)
  • Brachial artery here = where the BP cuff auscultates
Arterial access & Allen’s test
  • Radial artery — site for ABGs & arterial lines
  • Allen’s test first: confirm ulnar collateral supply via the palmar arches before cannulating the radial
Forearm compartment syndrome → Volkmann’s ischaemic contracture. Classically follows a supracondylar fracture injuring the brachial artery. Rising compartment pressure → muscle ischaemia → the 6 Ps (Pain out of proportion & on passive stretch, Paraesthesia, Pallor, Pulselessness [late], Paralysis, Perishingly cold). Untreated → fibrosis & a fixed flexion contracture of the wrist & fingers. Treatment is emergency fasciotomy — do not wait for a lost pulse.
The Axilla & Lymphatic Drainage
Axillary nodes
  • Drain the upper limb and ~75% of the breast
  • Grouped in levels I–III relative to pectoralis minor (I below, II behind, III above)
  • First staging site for breast cancer spread → sentinel node biopsy
Cost of axillary clearance
  • Lymphoedema of the arm (disrupted drainage)
  • Intercostobrachial nerve injury → numb medial upper arm
  • Long thoracic nerve → winged scapula
  • Thoracodorsal nerve → weak latissimus dorsi
⭐ Exam Pearls
Site predicts nerve: surgical neck → axillary; midshaft → radial (wrist drop); supracondylar → median + brachial artery; medial epicondyle → ulnar.
Benediction (median, on making a fist) vs claw (ulnar, at rest) — the classic pair to distinguish.
Ulnar paradox: the higher the lesion, the less the claw — because medial FDP is also out.
Erb’s = C5–C6 “waiter’s tip”; Klumpke’s = C8–T1 claw hand ± Horner’s.
Snuffbox tenderness = scaphoid # until proven otherwise; normal first X-ray does NOT exclude it — splint & re-image.
CTS spares thenar skin sensation (palmar cutaneous branch bypasses the tunnel) but wastes the thenar muscles.
Always document axillary-nerve function before AND after reducing a dislocated shoulder.
Compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis — pain on passive stretch is the earliest sign; fasciotomy before the pulse disappears.
UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements:
Why this matters: upper-limb muscles are best learned by compartment, because a compartment shares a nerve, an action and a blood supply. If you know a muscle lives in the anterior forearm, you already know it is a flexor/pronator supplied by the median nerve (with two ulnar exceptions). Learn the compartment → nerve → action logic and individual muscles slot into place — and every “which nerve is injured?” question becomes answerable.
The Big Picture — Compartments & Their Nerves

Six functional groups run the whole limb. Fix this table first; the rest of the note simply fills in each row.

Region / compartmentNerveRoot valueOverall action
Anterior arm (flexors)MusculocutaneousC5–C7Flex elbow & shoulder; supinate
Posterior arm (extensor)RadialC5–T1Extend elbow
Anterior forearm (flexors/pronators)Median (+ ulnar ×2)C6–T1Flex wrist/fingers; pronate
Posterior forearm (extensors)Radial (deep branch / PIN)C5–T1Extend wrist/fingers; supinate

The two golden rules. (1) Anterior = flexor, posterior = extensor throughout the limb. (2) The median nerve owns the anterior forearm and thenar hand except for 1½ muscles in the forearm (FCU + medial half of FDP) and most intrinsics — those are ulnar. The whole extensor side is radial. Get these territories and you can localise any lesion.
Muscles of the Pectoral Girdle — Connecting Trunk to Scapula

These “axio-appendicular” muscles anchor the scapula and clavicle to the trunk. A mobile, well-anchored scapula is the platform every arm movement is built on.

Anterior group
  • Pectoralis major — flexes, adducts & medially rotates the arm (medial & lateral pectoral nerves)
  • Pectoralis minor — protracts & depresses the scapula (medial pectoral nerve)
  • Serratus anterior — protracts the scapula & holds it to the chest wall; rotates it up for abduction >90° (long thoracic nerve → palsy = winged scapula)
  • Subclavius — steadies/depresses the clavicle
Posterior group (superficial back)
  • Trapezius — elevates (upper), retracts (middle) & depresses (lower) the scapula; rotates it up (accessory nerve CN XI)
  • Latissimus dorsi — extends, adducts & medially rotates the arm — “the handcuff / swimmer’s muscle” (thoracodorsal nerve)
  • Levator scapulae — elevates the scapula (dorsal scapular n. + C3–C4)
  • Rhomboid major & minor — retract & rotate the scapula down (dorsal scapular nerve)
Force couples rotate the scapula. To lift the arm above the head the glenoid must point upward. Trapezius (upper + lower fibres) and serratus anterior pull in a coordinated couple to rotate the scapula up ~60°. Lose serratus anterior (long thoracic n.) and the patient can’t abduct past ~90° and the scapula wings.
Scapulohumeral Muscles — Moving the Shoulder Itself
Deltoid & teres major
  • Deltoid — the main abductor (15–90°); anterior fibres flex/medially rotate, posterior fibres extend/laterally rotate (axillary nerve)
  • Teres major — adducts & medially rotates the arm; an “assistant to lat dorsi” (lower subscapular nerve)
Rotator cuff — “SITS”
  • Supraspinatus — initiates abduction 0–15° (suprascapular n.); most-torn cuff muscle
  • Infraspinatus — lateral rotation (suprascapular n.)
  • Teres minor — lateral rotation (axillary n.)
  • Subscapularis — medial rotation (upper & lower subscapular nn.)
  • Together they are the dynamic stabilisers that hold the humeral head in the shallow glenoid

The abduction sequence — a favourite exam chain. 0–15° supraspinatus starts it → 15–90° deltoid takes over → 90–180° the scapula must rotate up (trapezius + serratus anterior force couple). So a supraspinatus tear = trouble initiating; an axillary nerve lesion = weak mid-range; a serratus/long-thoracic lesion = can’t get the arm overhead.
The Arm — Anterior & Posterior Compartments
Anterior arm — flexors (musculocutaneous n.)
  • Biceps brachii — supinates the flexed forearm (its strongest action) & flexes the elbow; long head from supraglenoid tubercle, short head from coracoid process; inserts on the radial tuberosity
  • Brachialis — the workhorse elbow flexor (flexes in every position); floor of the cubital fossa; inserts on the ulnar tuberosity
  • Coracobrachialis — flexes & adducts the arm; pierced by the musculocutaneous nerve
Posterior arm — extensor (radial n.)
  • Triceps brachii — the main elbow extensor; three heads — long (infraglenoid tubercle, also extends/adducts the shoulder), lateral & medial (humerus); inserts on the olecranon
  • Anconeus — assists extension & stabilises the elbow during pronation/supination
Biceps is a supinator first, flexor second. This is why you flex and supinate to turn a stiff screw or a corkscrew (right-handed). Brachialis does the pure flexing, so the biceps can be spared for supination. Test biceps power against resisted supination, not just flexion.

FDS vs FDP — how to test them. FDS flexes the PIP: hold the other fingers straight (to neutralise the common FDP belly) and ask the patient to bend the middle joint. FDP flexes the DIP: stabilise the middle phalanx and ask them to bend the fingertip. The anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) supplies FPL, pronator quadratus & lateral FDP — an AIN palsy gives the classic inability to make an “OK” sign (weak pinch of thumb + index).

The “mobile wad” & the wrist-drop logic. Brachioradialis + ECRL + ECRB form the lateral mobile wad. Because the extensors are all radial-supplied, a high radial lesion → wrist drop. A PIN lesion spares ECRL (branches off high) & wrist extension, so the wrist stays up (deviating radially, as the PIN-supplied ECU is lost) but the fingers drop — a subtle but classic distinction.
Intrinsic Muscles of the Hand

Small muscles wholly within the hand. The ulnar nerve runs the show — it supplies all intrinsics except the thenar muscles and the lateral two lumbricals, which are median (recall “LOAF”).

Thenar & hypothenar
  • Thenar (median, recurrent branch): opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis — position & oppose the thumb
  • Hypothenar (ulnar): opponens digiti minimi, abductor digiti minimi, flexor digiti minimi brevis — cup the little finger
  • Adductor pollicis (ulnar, deep branch) — adducts the thumb → tested by Froment’s sign
Lumbricals & interossei
  • 4 lumbricals — flex MCP & extend the IP joints (lateral 2 = median, medial 2 = ulnar)
  • Dorsal interossei (4) — ABduct the fingers: “DAB” (ulnar)
  • Palmar interossei (3) — ADduct the fingers: “PAD” (ulnar)
LOAF = the median-supplied intrinsics. Lateral two lumbricals, Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis. Everything else intrinsic is ulnar — which is why an ulnar lesion devastates fine grip while the thumb’s pincer (median) is preserved.

🧠 Mnemonics
Rotator cuff = “SITS” — Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres minor, Subscapularis.
Median intrinsics = “LOAF” — Lumbricals 1&2, Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis.
Interossei — DAB = Dorsal ABduct; PAD = Palmar ADduct.
Ulnar ½ muscles in forearm — FCU + medial half of FDP. Everything else anterior = median.
AIN supplies — FPL, Pronator quadratus, lateral FDP → the “OK sign” muscles.
Lumbricals — “flex the knuckle, straighten the finger” (flex MCP, extend IP).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Compartment tells you the nerve: anterior arm = musculocutaneous, posterior arm = radial, anterior forearm = median (+ulnar ×1½), posterior forearm = radial/PIN.
Brachialis is the true workhorse of elbow flexion; biceps is primarily a supinator of the flexed forearm.
Abduction chain: supraspinatus 0–15° → deltoid 15–90° → scapular rotation (trapezius+serratus) 90–180°.
Serratus anterior (long thoracic n.) both protracts the scapula and rotates it up — its loss = winged scapula + can’t abduct overhead.
FDS flexes PIP, FDP flexes DIP — test them separately by isolating the joint.
PIN lesion → finger drop with preserved wrist extension (ECRL spared); high radial lesion → full wrist drop.
Froment’s sign tests adductor pollicis (ulnar); the patient substitutes FPL (median) to hold paper.
Palmaris longus is absent in ~15% of people and is a classic tendon-graft donor.
UPPER LIMB__Nerves:
Why this matters: every motor and sensory question about the upper limb traces back to one structure — the brachial plexus and its five terminal branches. Learn the plexus as a map (roots → trunks → divisions → cords → branches), then follow each terminal nerve along its course, noting where it is vulnerable, what it moves and what it feels. Do that and both anatomy spotters and clinical “where’s the lesion?” questions become one and the same.
The Brachial Plexus — The Master Map

Formed from the anterior rami of C5–T1. Five stages, each with its own branches. Memorise the skeleton first: Roots → Trunks → Divisions → Cords → Branches (“Randy Travis Drinks Cold Beer”).

StageComponentsBranches given off
Roots (C5–T1)5 anterior ramiDorsal scapular (C5 → rhomboids, levator scapulae); long thoracic (C5–C7 → serratus anterior)
TrunksUpper (C5–C6), Middle (C7), Lower (C8–T1)From the upper trunk only: suprascapular (C5–C6 → supra/infraspinatus) & nerve to subclavius
DivisionsEach trunk → anterior + posterior division (6 total)None (“no branches from divisions”)
CordsLateral, Posterior, Medial (named by position around the axillary artery)See below — each cord gives collateral branches then terminal nerves
Branches5 terminal nervesMusculocutaneous, Axillary, Radial, Median, Ulnar
Cord branches — learn them by cord. Lateral cord (“LLM”): lateral pectoral, lateral root of median, musculocutaneous. Medial cord: medial pectoral, medial cutaneous nerve of arm, medial cutaneous nerve of forearm, ulnar, medial root of median. Posterior cord (“ULTRA”): upper subscapular, lower subscapular, thoracodorsal, radial, axillary. The median nerve is formed by a lateral + medial root straddling the axillary artery (the “M” of the plexus).
The Five Terminal Nerves — Course, Motor & Sensory
Nerve (roots)MotorSensory (cutaneous)
Musculocutaneous (C5–C7)Anterior arm — coracobrachialis, biceps, brachialisContinues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of forearm
Axillary (C5–C6)Deltoid, teres minorUpper lateral cutaneous nerve of arm — “regimental badge”
Median (C6–T1)Most anterior forearm flexors; thenar muscles & lateral 2 lumbricals (the LOAF group)Palmar lateral 3½ fingers + adjacent palm
Radial (C5–T1)Triceps; then all extensors (BR & ECRL from the radial trunk, the rest via the PIN)Posterior arm/forearm; dorsal lateral 3½ fingers (proximal)
Ulnar (C8–T1)FCU + medial ½ FDP; most intrinsic hand musclesPalmar & dorsal medial 1½ fingers
Musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C7)
  • From the lateral cord; pierces coracobrachialis
  • Runs between biceps & brachialis supplying all three anterior-arm flexors
  • Emerges lateral to the biceps tendon as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm
  • Injury (rare): weak elbow flexion/supination + lost lateral forearm sensation
Axillary nerve (C5–C6)
  • From the posterior cord; passes through the quadrangular space with the posterior circumflex humeral artery
  • Wraps the surgical neck of the humerus → at risk in fractures & anterior shoulder dislocation
  • Motor: deltoid + teres minor; Sensory: “regimental badge” over the deltoid
  • Always test deltoid power & badge sensation before/after reducing a shoulder
Median nerve (C6–T1)
  • Lateral + medial roots straddle the axillary artery; runs down the arm giving no branches in the arm
  • Enters the cubital fossa (medial to brachial artery) → between the heads of pronator teres
  • Gives the anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) → FPL, PQ, lateral FDP
  • Enters the hand through the carpal tunnel → thenar (recurrent branch) + lateral 2 lumbricals
  • Palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the tunnel → thenar skin spared in CTS
Ulnar nerve (C8–T1)
  • From the medial cord; passes behind the medial epicondyle (cubital tunnel — the “funny bone”)
  • Forearm: supplies FCU + medial ½ FDP only
  • Enters the hand via Guyon’s canal (superficial to the flexor retinaculum)
  • Supplies all intrinsics except LOAF: hypothenar, interossei, medial 2 lumbricals, adductor pollicis
  • Dorsal cutaneous branch leaves proximally → spared in Guyon’s canal lesions
Radial nerve (C5–T1) — the great extensor nerve
  • Largest branch of the posterior cord; spirals down the radial (spiral) groove of the humerus with the profunda brachii artery
  • Motor in the arm: triceps (+ anconeus); pierces the lateral intermuscular septum to reach the anterior compartment at the elbow
  • At the elbow it divides into a superficial (sensory) branch and a deep branch → posterior interosseous nerve (PIN)
  • PIN pierces supinator (arcade of Frohse) to supply the extensors — but note brachioradialis & ECRL branch earlier, from the radial trunk
  • Sensory: posterior arm/forearm + dorsum of the lateral 3½ digits (proximal to the nail beds)
Cutaneous Innervation — Peripheral Nerve Territories

Each patch of skin has two answers: the peripheral nerve that carries it and the dermatome (root) it belongs to. Lesions of a nerve and of a root give different, diagnostic patterns.

Region of skinPeripheral nerve
Lateral shoulder (“regimental badge”)Axillary (upper lateral cutaneous n. of arm)
Medial arm & axillaMedial cutaneous n. of arm + intercostobrachial (T2)
Lateral forearmMusculocutaneous (lateral cutaneous n. of forearm)
Medial forearmMedial cutaneous n. of forearm
Posterior arm / forearmRadial (posterior cutaneous nn.)
Palmar lateral 3½ digitsMedian
Palmar & dorsal medial 1½ digitsUlnar
Dorsum lateral 3½ digits (proximal)Radial (superficial branch)
Dermatomes of the Upper Limb

A dermatome is the strip of skin supplied by a single spinal nerve root. The limb’s dermatomes sweep from the lateral shoulder (C5) round to the medial arm (T1–T2). Learn the fingertip landmarks — they are the fastest way to pin a root.

C5 — lateral arm (over deltoid / regimental badge)
C6 — lateral forearm & the thumb
C7 — the middle finger
C8 — the little finger & medial hand
T1 — medial forearm
T2 — medial arm & axilla
Fingertip landmarks (learn cold). Thumb = C6, middle finger = C7, little finger = C8. Count across the hand 6-7-8. For the arm: “reach for C6, salute at C5” — the thumb-up hitchhiker points to C6.
Nerve vs Root Lesions — Telling Them Apart
Peripheral nerve lesion
  • Sensory loss follows the peripheral nerve territory (e.g. median = lateral 3½ palmar digits)
  • Motor loss maps to that nerve’s muscles
  • Sharp, well-defined borders
Root (dermatome) lesion
  • Sensory loss follows a dermatomal strip (e.g. C6 = thumb, running up the forearm)
  • Weakness maps to a myotome (crosses several nerves) + lost reflex
  • Cause: disc prolapse / foraminal stenosis (radiculopathy)
Reflex root values. Biceps & brachioradialis = C5–C6; triceps = C7. A lost biceps jerk with thumb numbness points to a C6 root; a lost triceps jerk with middle-finger numbness points to C7.
Sympathetic Supply & Horner's Syndrome

The limb’s sympathetic fibres (vasomotor, sudomotor, pilomotor) arrive via T2–T6 segments, relay in the sympathetic chain and travel with the plexus. Because T1 lies at the base of the plexus, a lower plexus (Klumpke’s) injury or a Pancoast apical lung tumour can drag in the T1 sympathetic fibres.

Horner’s syndrome = ptosis, miosis & anhidrosis (± enophthalmos) from interruption of the sympathetic supply to the head. Its appearance alongside a lower-trunk plexus lesion (hand intrinsic weakness) is a red flag for a Pancoast tumour at the lung apex.
🧠 Mnemonics
Plexus skeleton — “Randy Travis Drinks Cold Beer” = Roots, Trunks, Divisions, Cords, Branches.
Terminal branches — “MARMU” = Musculocutaneous, Axillary, Radial, Median, Ulnar.
Posterior cord — “ULTRA” = Upper subscapular, Lower subscapular, Thoracodorsal, Radial, Axillary.
Lateral cord — “LLM” = Lateral pectoral, Lateral root of median, Musculocutaneous.
Fingertips — thumb C6, middle C7, little C8 (count 6-7-8 across).
Only branches above the cords — dorsal scapular & long thoracic (roots); suprascapular & n. to subclavius (upper trunk).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Cords are named (lateral/posterior/medial) by their position around the axillary artery.
The median nerve has a lateral + medial root — the “M” sitting on the axillary artery.
Long thoracic (C5–C7) & suprascapular are the classic “above-the-cords” nerves examiners love.
Axillary nerve = quadrangular space + surgical neck → test the regimental badge after any shoulder injury.
Median gives NO branches in the arm; the AIN is its main forearm motor branch.
Ulnar dorsal cutaneous branch leaves proximal to the wrist → intact sensation over the dorsomedial hand localises a lesion to Guyon’s canal.
Radial superficial branch = sensory (dorsal hand); deep branch = PIN = motor to the extensors.
Horner’s + wasted hand intrinsics = think Pancoast tumour / lower plexus (T1).
UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints:
Why this matters: bones are the map on which everything else is drawn — every muscle attaches to a named landmark, every nerve grooves a named surface, every fracture is described by the feature it breaks. Learn the landmarks (they are the attachment points) and the joints (their type dictates the movements), and the rest of the limb hangs off this scaffold.
The Skeleton — Overview

The upper limb has two parts: the pectoral (shoulder) girdle that anchors it to the trunk, and the free limb.

Pectoral girdle
  • Clavicle — the only bony strut between limb & axial skeleton
  • Scapula — a mobile platform gliding on the chest wall
Free limb
  • Arm: humerus
  • Forearm: radius (lateral) & ulna (medial)
  • Hand: 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges
Clavicle
Features
  • S-shaped; medial (sternal) end convex forward, lateral (acromial) end concave forward
  • Superior surface smooth; inferior surface rough for ligaments — conoid tubercle & trapezoid line (coracoclavicular ligament) laterally, impression for costoclavicular ligament medially, subclavian groove (subclavius) in between
Clinical & development
  • First bone to ossify (~5th week, intramembranous) and one of the last to finish (medial epiphysis fuses ~25 yr)
  • Commonest fracture site = junction of the middle and lateral thirds; medial fragment pulled up by sternocleidomastoid
Scapula
Borders, angles & fossae
  • Borders: superior, medial (vertebral), lateral (axillary)
  • Angles: superior, inferior, lateral (bears the glenoid)
  • Fossae: supraspinous & infraspinous (posterior, split by the spine); subscapular (anterior/costal)
Processes & the glenoid
  • Spine → continues as the acromion (forms the AC joint)
  • Coracoid process — “lighthouse of the shoulder” (pec minor, coracobrachialis, short head biceps)
  • Glenoid cavity — shallow; supraglenoid tubercle (long head biceps) & infraglenoid tubercle (long head triceps)
  • Suprascapular notch — suprascapular nerve passes under the transverse scapular ligament
Humerus
RegionLandmarksClinical note
ProximalHead, anatomical neck, greater & lesser tubercles, intertubercular (bicipital) groove, surgical neckSurgical neck # → axillary nerve
ShaftDeltoid tuberosity (lateral), radial (spiral) groove (posterior)Mid-shaft # → radial nerve (wrist drop)
DistalTrochlea (→ ulna) & capitulum (→ radial head); medial & lateral epicondyles; coronoid & radial fossae (front), olecranon fossa (back)Medial epicondyle → ulnar nerve; supracondylar # (children) → median n. & brachial artery
Radius & Ulna
Radius (lateral)
  • Head (disc-shaped, rotates in the radial notch) → neck → radial tuberosity (biceps insertion)
  • Distal end is expanded: styloid process (lateral), ulnar notch (medial), dorsal (Lister’s) tubercle — EPL hooks around it
  • The radius does the “carrying” — most of the wrist joint sits on it
Ulna (medial)
  • Proximal: olecranon & coronoid process enclose the trochlear notch; radial notch laterally; ulnar tuberosity (brachialis)
  • Distal: small head + styloid process (medial) — the ulna does not reach the wrist joint (separated by the articular disc)
Styloid rule: the radial styloid lies ~1 cm distal to the ulnar styloid. Loss of this relationship suggests a distal radius fracture (e.g. Colles’) with shortening.
Carpus, Metacarpals & Phalanges

Eight carpal bones in two rows (lateral → medial). Learn them with “Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can’t Handle.”

RowBones (lateral → medial)
ProximalScaphoid, Lunate, Triquetrum, Pisiform
DistalTrapezium, Trapezoid, Capitate, Hamate
Scaphoid — most commonly fractured carpal; snuffbox tenderness; risk of AVN (retrograde supply).
Lunate — most commonly dislocated carpal; can cause acute carpal tunnel syndrome.
Hook of hamate & pisiform — form the medial wall of Guyon’s canal (ulnar nerve).
Trapezium — saddle joint with the 1st metacarpal → thumb opposition.

Distal to the carpus: 5 metacarpals (numbered 1–5 from the thumb) and 14 phalanges — the thumb has 2 (proximal & distal), each finger has 3 (proximal, middle, distal).

The Glenohumeral (Shoulder) Joint

A multiaxial ball-and-socket joint — the price of its huge range is instability (the most commonly dislocated joint).

Articulation & static stabilisers
  • Large humeral head on a small, shallow glenoid — deepened ~50% by the fibrocartilaginous glenoid labrum
  • Loose fibrous capsule (lax inferiorly — the weak point → inferior/anterior dislocation)
  • Glenohumeral ligaments (superior/middle/inferior) & the coracohumeral ligament reinforce the capsule
  • Coraco-acromial arch (coracoid + acromion + ligament) prevents superior dislocation
Dynamic stabilisers
  • The rotator cuff (SITS) hugs the head into the glenoid through range
  • The long head of biceps tendon runs through the joint (intracapsular, extrasynovial)
  • Bursae: subacromial/subdeltoid bursa cushions the cuff — inflamed in impingement
Dislocation. ~95% are anterior (arm abducted + externally rotated) → risks the axillary nerve (test the regimental badge). A Bankart lesion (labral tear) and a Hill–Sachs lesion (posterolateral humeral head dent) predispose to recurrence.
The Elbow & Radioulnar Joints
Elbow joint (hinge)
  • Two articulations in one capsule: humero-ulnar (trochlea ↔ trochlear notch) & humero-radial (capitulum ↔ radial head)
  • Stabilised by the ulnar (medial) collateral ligament — its anterior band resists valgus — and the radial (lateral) collateral ligament
  • Carrying angle ~5–15° valgus (greater in females); lost/reversed (“gunstock”) after malunited supracondylar fractures
Radioulnar joints (pivot)
  • Proximal: radial head spins within the annular ligament against the radial notch of the ulna
  • Distal: ulnar head against the ulnar notch of the radius, with the articular disc (TFCC)
  • Linked by the interosseous membrane → together give pronation/supination and transmit load radius↔ulna
Pulled elbow (nursemaid’s elbow). A sharp pull on a toddler’s pronated forearm subluxes the radial head out of the annular ligament. The child holds the arm flexed & pronated; reduction by supination/flexion.
The Wrist & Joints of the Hand
Wrist (radiocarpal)
  • Ellipsoid joint: distal radius + articular disc articulate with scaphoid, lunate & triquetrum
  • The ulna does not take part directly (buffered by the TFCC)
  • Movements: flexion/extension & radial/ulnar deviation (ulnar > radial)
Carpometacarpal, MCP & IP
  • 1st CMC (thumb): saddle joint (trapezium–MC1) → opposition; common site of OA (squaring of the thumb base)
  • CMC 2–5: plane joints (little movement)
  • MCP: condyloid — flex/ext + abd/add (collateral ligaments tight in flexion)
  • IP (PIP & DIP): hinge — flexion/extension only
Ossification & the Paediatric Elbow — CRITOE

Long bones ossify from a primary (diaphyseal) centre plus secondary (epiphyseal) centres. The clavicle ossifies first of all (intramembranous). The six elbow ossification centres appear in a fixed order — vital for reading a child’s elbow X-ray without mistaking a centre for a fracture.

CRITOE (appearing roughly at ages 1-3-5-7-9-11): Capitellum → Radial head → Internal (medial) epicondyle → Trochlea → Olecranon → External (lateral) epicondyle. If the trochlea looks ossified but you can’t see the internal epicondyle, suspect an avulsed medial epicondyle trapped in the joint.
🧠 Mnemonics
Carpal bones — “Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can’t Handle” (Scaphoid, Lunate, Triquetrum, Pisiform / Trapezium, Trapezoid, Capitate, Hamate).
Elbow ossification — CRITOE (Capitellum, Radial head, Internal epicondyle, Trochlea, Olecranon, External epicondyle) at 1-3-5-7-9-11.
Trapezium vs trapezoid — the trapeziuM sits under the thuMb.
Joint-type shortcuts — shoulder = ball-and-socket; elbow & IP = hinge; radioulnar = pivot; thumb CMC = saddle; wrist = ellipsoid; MCP = condyloid.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Fracture site → nerve: surgical neck = axillary; mid-shaft/spiral groove = radial; medial epicondyle = ulnar; supracondylar = median + brachial artery.
The clavicle is the only bony connection of the upper limb to the axial skeleton (via the sternoclavicular joint).
Scaphoid = most fractured carpal (snuffbox tenderness, AVN risk); lunate = most commonly dislocated.
Glenohumeral joint is weakest inferiorly → dislocations go anterior/inferior; always check the axillary nerve.
The ulna does not reach the wrist joint — the radius + TFCC carry the carpus.
1st CMC (thumb) is a saddle joint — its shape allows opposition and it is a common site of osteoarthritis.
CRITOE order lets you avoid calling a normal ossification centre a fracture on a child’s elbow film.
Pulled elbow = radial head slips from the annular ligament; reduce by supination + flexion.
